ser-vs-estar.why: Location of people and things takes estar.
Professions take ser.

ser-vs-estar.en: The party is at my house.
ser-vs-estar.why: Where an event takes place uses ser.
A temporary condition takes estar.
Dates and days take ser.
States and moods take estar.
With ser, aburrido means boring. With estar it means bored.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Aburrido: boring with ser, bored with estar

ser-vs-estar.why: Listo means ready with estar and clever with ser.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Listo: clever with ser, ready with estar

ser-vs-estar.why: Even permanent locations take estar.
Muerto takes estar, even though death is permanent.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Muerto takes estar, even though death is permanent

ser-vs-estar.why: Rico means wealthy with ser and delicious with estar.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Rico: wealthy with ser, delicious with estar

ser-vs-estar.why: Actions in progress use estar with the gerund.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Actions in progress, with the gerund

ser-vs-estar.why: Origin takes ser.
A trait that says what someone is like takes ser.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Traits that describe what something is like

ser-vs-estar.why: Time takes ser.
Possession takes ser.

ser-vs-estar.en: The concert is at the stadium.
ser-vs-estar.why: Where an event takes place uses ser.
A place's location takes estar. Only events take ser.
Location of things takes estar.
Being sick is a condition, so estar.

ser-vs-estar.q: Hoy _____ muy nerviosa. (ser or estar, yo)
ser-vs-estar.why: A mood right now takes estar.
An action in progress uses estar with the gerund.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Actions in progress, with the gerund

ser-vs-estar.q: No hay nada que hacer. _____ aburrido.
ser-vs-estar.en: There's nothing to do. I'm bored.
ser-vs-estar.why: With estar, aburrido means bored. Soy aburrido would mean I'm boring.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Aburrido: boring with ser, bored with estar

ser-vs-estar.q: Tu hija _____ muy lista. Siempre saca buenas notas.
ser-vs-estar.en: Your daughter is very clever. She always gets good grades.
ser-vs-estar.why: With ser, listo means clever.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Listo: clever with ser, ready with estar

ser-vs-estar.why: With estar, rico means delicious.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Rico: wealthy with ser, delicious with estar

ser-vs-estar.en: Don't drink that milk. It's gone off.
ser-vs-estar.why: With estar, malo means sick or gone off.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Malo: bad with ser, sick or gone off with estar

ser-vs-estar.q: Ese perro _____ malo. Muerde a todos.
ser-vs-estar.en: That dog is mean. It bites everyone.
ser-vs-estar.why: With ser, malo describes what the dog is like.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Malo: bad with ser, sick or gone off with estar

ser-vs-estar.why: In everyday speech, casado usually takes estar.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Casado usually takes estar in everyday speech

ser-vs-estar.q: Mi mamá _____ contenta con la noticia.
ser-vs-estar.en: My mom is happy about the news.
ser-vs-estar.why: Contento always takes estar.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Contento always takes estar, but feliz can take either

ser-vs-estar.why: Muerto takes estar.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Muerto takes estar, even though death is permanent

ser-vs-estar.why: Origin takes ser.

por-vs-para.en: This gift is for you.
We walked along the seawall.
por-vs-para.why: Movement through or along takes por.

por-vs-para.en: I paid ten dollars for the shirt.
We're leaving for Havana.
The homework is due Monday.
I was late because of the traffic.
I study in order to learn.
I lived there for five years.
For me, it's very expensive.
I'll call you on the phone.
I work for a big company.
por-vs-para.rule: The choice can change what you're saying

por-vs-para.en: We finally arrived.
por-vs-para.why: Por fin is a set phrase.
por-vs-para.rule: These are worth memorizing as units

por-vs-para.en: This book is for my brother.
por-vs-para.why: The person who gets it takes para.

por-vs-para.en: I'm saving money to buy a car.

por-vs-para.q: El avión sale _____ Bogotá a las seis.
por-vs-para.en: The plane leaves for Bogotá at six.
I need the answer by Friday.
For her age, she speaks very well.
por-vs-para.why: A comparison like for her age takes para.

por-vs-para.en: They canceled the game because of the rain.
por-vs-para.why: The rain is the cause, so por.

por-vs-para.q: Pasamos _____ tu casa, pero no estabas.
por-vs-para.en: We went by your house, but you weren't there.
por-vs-para.why: Going by or through a place takes por.

por-vs-para.q: Te doy mi bicicleta _____ tu guitarra.
por-vs-para.en: I'll give you my bike for your guitar.

por-vs-para.q: Estuvimos en la playa _____ dos semanas.
por-vs-para.en: We were at the beach for two weeks.
por-vs-para.why: How long something lasted takes por.

por-vs-para.en: I sent the package by air.
por-vs-para.why: The means of transport takes por.

por-vs-para.q: No puedo ir. ¿Puedes ir tú _____ mí?
por-vs-para.en: I can't go. Can you go in my place?
por-vs-para.why: In someone's place, or on their behalf, is por.

por-vs-para.en: I did it all for my kids' sake.

por-vs-para.q: La cena fue preparada _____ mi abuela.
por-vs-para.en: Dinner was made by my grandmother.
por-vs-para.why: In the passive, by is por.

por-vs-para.q: _____ ejemplo, el mango y la papaya.
por-vs-para.en: For example, mango and papaya.
por-vs-para.why: Por ejemplo is a set phrase.
por-vs-para.rule: These are worth memorizing as units

por-vs-para.en: I was tired. That's why I didn't go.
por-vs-para.rule: These are worth memorizing as units

por-vs-para.en: I work in place of my uncle.
por-vs-para.why: Por mi tío means in his place. Para mi tío would mean he's your boss.
por-vs-para.rule: The choice can change what you're saying

por-vs-para.q: Trabajo _____ mi tía. Ella es la dueña de la tienda.
por-vs-para.en: I work for my aunt. She owns the store.
por-vs-para.rule: The choice can change what you're saying

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: Yesterday I ate chicken and rice.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: A completed action takes the preterite.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Completed actions

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: As a child I used to play in the street.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Habits take the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Habits: used to, would

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: It was ten o'clock when I arrived.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Time in the past takes the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Time and age in the past

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: Suddenly the power went out.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Sudden events take the preterite.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Sudden changes or interruptions

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: The interruption takes the preterite, and the background takes the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: The imperfect is the background, and the preterite is what happened

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: It was raining when we left.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Leaving is the event, set against the background of the rain.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: The imperfect is the background, and the preterite is what happened

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I lived in Cuba for twenty years.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: A defined period takes the preterite, however long.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: A defined period of time, however long

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: _____ a mi esposa en un baile.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I met my wife at a dance.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Conocer in the preterite means met.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Conocer: met in the preterite, knew in the imperfect

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I already knew the truth.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Saber in the imperfect means knew. In the preterite it means found out.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Saber: found out in the preterite, knew in the imperfect

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I was cooking while she was reading.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Two actions in progress both take the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Actions in progress in the past

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I finally managed to sleep.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Poder in the preterite means managed to.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Poder: managed to in the preterite, was able to in the imperfect

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: Hacía sol y la playa _____ llena.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: It was sunny and the beach was full.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Description and background take the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Description and background

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: He refused to come.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: No querer in the preterite means refused.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: No querer in the preterite means refused

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: Last night I watched a really good movie.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: A finished action last night takes the preterite.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Completed actions

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I studied in Chile for three years.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: A set period, however long, takes the preterite.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: A defined period of time, however long

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: La fiesta _____ hasta las dos de la mañana.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: The party lasted until two in the morning.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: It lasted a set time, then ended, so the preterite.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: A defined period of time, however long

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: Me levanté, me duché y _____ al trabajo.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I got up, showered and went to work.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: One event after another takes the preterite.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: A series of events that move a story forward

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: Abrió la puerta, _____ y se sentó.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: He opened the door, came in and sat down.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Events that move the story forward take the preterite.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: A series of events that move a story forward

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: Suddenly it started to rain.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: De repente signals a sudden change, so the preterite.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Sudden changes or interruptions

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: Todos los veranos _____ a la playa.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: Every summer we used to go to the beach.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Todos los veranos is a habit, so the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Habits: used to, would

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: My grandfather always used to tell us stories.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Siempre with something that used to happen takes the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Habits: used to, would

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: La casa _____ pequeña y tenía un jardín.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: The house was small and had a garden.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Describing the house is background, so the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Description and background

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: _____ frío y no había nadie en la calle.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: It was cold and there was nobody in the street.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Weather setting the scene is background, so the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Description and background

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: While I was working, the kids were playing.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Two actions in progress at the same time take the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Actions in progress in the past

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: When I got married, I was twenty-five.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Age in the past takes the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Time and age in the past

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: Caminaba por el parque cuando _____ a mi profesor.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I was walking through the park when I saw my teacher.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Caminaba is the background, and seeing him is what happened.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: The imperfect is the background, and the preterite is what happened

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: When you arrived, I was making dinner.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Making dinner was going on when you arrived, so the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: The imperfect is the background, and the preterite is what happened

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: Ya _____ a su familia antes de la boda.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I already knew his family before the wedding.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Knowing someone over time takes the imperfect. Conocí would mean I met.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Conocer: met in the preterite, knew in the imperfect

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: Yesterday I found out you were sick.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: In the preterite, saber means found out.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Saber: found out in the preterite, knew in the imperfect

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: _____ llamarte, pero no tenía tu número.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I wanted to call you, but I didn't have your number.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Wanting to, as a state, is the imperfect. Quise would mean I tried.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Querer: tried to in the preterite, wanted to in the imperfect

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: Le pedí ayuda, pero no _____ ayudarme.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I asked her for help, but she refused to help me.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: No quiso means refused.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: No querer in the preterite means refused

subjunctive.en: I want you to come.
subjunctive.why: A wish plus a new subject takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: A trigger in the main clause, then que, then a new subject

subjunctive.en: I think it's true.
subjunctive.why: Creo que states a belief, so it takes the indicative.
subjunctive.rule: Doubt and denial

subjunctive.en: I don't think it's true.
subjunctive.why: No creer expresses doubt, so it takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Doubt and denial

subjunctive.en: Call me when you arrive.
subjunctive.why: Cuando takes the subjunctive for something that hasn't happened yet.
subjunctive.rule: Time words, when the event hasn't happened yet

subjunctive.q: Cuando _____ a casa, siempre te llamo.
subjunctive.en: When I get home, I always call you.
subjunctive.why: For habits, cuando takes the indicative.
subjunctive.rule: Time words, when the event hasn't happened yet

subjunctive.en: I hope you have a good trip.
subjunctive.why: Esperar que expresses a wish.
subjunctive.rule: Wishes and requests

subjunctive.en: I hope it doesn't rain.
subjunctive.why: Ojalá always takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Wishes and requests

subjunctive.en: I'm looking for an apartment that has a balcony.
subjunctive.why: You haven't found it yet, so it may not exist.
subjunctive.rule: Looking for something that may not exist

subjunctive.en: I have an apartment that has a balcony.
subjunctive.why: A known, real thing takes the indicative.
subjunctive.rule: Looking for something that may not exist

subjunctive.en: If I had money, I would travel.
subjunctive.why: Unreal conditions use si + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional.
subjunctive.rule: Unreal conditions: si + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional

subjunctive.en: We'll leave before it rains.
subjunctive.why: Antes de que always takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Purpose and conditions: para que, a menos que, sin que, antes de que

subjunctive.en: It's true that he's coming tomorrow.
subjunctive.why: Stating a fact takes the indicative.
subjunctive.rule: Doubt and denial

subjunctive.en: I want to come.
subjunctive.why: With no change of subject, use the infinitive.
subjunctive.rule: A trigger in the main clause, then que, then a new subject

subjunctive.q: Mis padres quieren que yo _____ medicina. (estudiar)
subjunctive.en: My parents want me to study medicine.
subjunctive.why: A wish, then que and a new subject, takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: A trigger in the main clause, then que, then a new subject

subjunctive.en: I need to leave early.
subjunctive.why: Same subject, so the infinitive, with no que.
subjunctive.rule: A trigger in the main clause, then que, then a new subject

subjunctive.en: I'm asking you to help me.
subjunctive.why: A request takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Wishes and requests

subjunctive.en: I hope they come tomorrow.
subjunctive.why: Ojalá always takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Wishes and requests

subjunctive.en: I'd rather you didn't get here late.
subjunctive.why: A preference about someone else takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Wishes and requests

subjunctive.en: I'm glad you're here.
subjunctive.why: An emotion about someone else takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Emotions

subjunctive.en: I'm sorry you can't come.
subjunctive.why: Siento que, for being sorry, takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Emotions

subjunctive.q: Me molesta que mi vecino _____ tanto ruido. (hacer)
subjunctive.en: It bothers me that my neighbor makes so much noise.
subjunctive.why: An emotion like me molesta takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Emotions

subjunctive.en: I doubt he'll arrive on time.
subjunctive.why: Doubt takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Doubt and denial

subjunctive.en: I'm sure you're right.
subjunctive.why: Certainty takes the indicative.
subjunctive.rule: Doubt and denial

subjunctive.en: It's important that you drink water.
subjunctive.why: Es importante que is a judgment, so the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Judgments with es + adjective

subjunctive.en: It might rain later.
subjunctive.why: Es posible que takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Judgments with es + adjective

subjunctive.en: It's obvious he doesn't feel like it.
subjunctive.why: Es obvio states a fact, so the indicative.
subjunctive.rule: Judgments with es + adjective

subjunctive.en: I'll wait for you until you finish.
subjunctive.why: You haven't finished yet, so hasta que takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Time words, when the event hasn't happened yet

subjunctive.en: When I grow up, I want to be a pilot.
subjunctive.why: It hasn't happened yet, so cuando takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Time words, when the event hasn't happened yet

subjunctive.q: Hablo despacio para que me _____. (entender, tú)
subjunctive.en: I speak slowly so that you understand me.
subjunctive.why: Para que always takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Purpose and conditions: para que, a menos que, sin que, antes de que

subjunctive.q: Vamos a la playa a menos que _____.
subjunctive.en: We'll go to the beach unless it rains.
subjunctive.why: A menos que always takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Purpose and conditions: para que, a menos que, sin que, antes de que

subjunctive.q: Siempre sale sin que nadie lo _____.
subjunctive.en: He always leaves without anyone seeing him.
subjunctive.why: Sin que always takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Purpose and conditions: para que, a menos que, sin que, antes de que

subjunctive.en: There's nobody who knows that.
subjunctive.why: Someone who doesn't exist takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Looking for something that may not exist

subjunctive.en: Do you know anyone who speaks French?
subjunctive.why: You don't know if such a person exists, so the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Looking for something that may not exist

subjunctive.en: I have a friend who speaks French.
subjunctive.why: A friend you know exists takes the indicative.
subjunctive.rule: Looking for something that may not exist

subjunctive.en: I wanted you to come with me.
subjunctive.why: A trigger in the past takes the imperfect subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: The same triggers, in the past

subjunctive.en: I'd like a coffee, please.
subjunctive.why: Quisiera is a polite way to ask.
subjunctive.rule: Polite requests

gender-and-plurals.why: Día is a masculine exception ending in -a.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Masculine nouns ending in -a, many from Greek and ending in -ma

gender-and-plurals.why: Mano is a feminine exception ending in -o.
Many nouns ending in -ma are masculine.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Masculine nouns ending in -a, many from Greek and ending in -ma

gender-and-plurals.why: Feminine nouns starting with stressed a take el in the singular. The adjective stays feminine.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Feminine nouns starting with a stressed a take el in the singular

gender-and-plurals.why: Mapa is a masculine exception ending in -a.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Masculine nouns ending in -a, many from Greek and ending in -ma

gender-and-plurals.why: Foto is short for fotografía, so it's feminine.

gender-and-plurals.en: one young person, two young people
gender-and-plurals.why: The accent appears to keep the stress on the same syllable.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Accents shift to keep the stress in place

gender-and-plurals.why: The accent drops because the stress is now regular.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Accents shift to keep the stress in place

reflexive-verbs.why: Yo takes me.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Me, te, se, nos, and se for ellos and ustedes

reflexive-verbs.why: Nosotros takes nos.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Me, te, se, nos, and se for ellos and ustedes

reflexive-verbs.why: The pronoun attaches to the infinitive, or goes before voy.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Attached to an infinitive or gerund, or before the verb in front of it

reflexive-verbs.why: Body parts take the, because the pronoun already shows whose they are.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Body parts and clothing take the, not my

reflexive-verbs.why: Irse means to leave.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Ir to go, irse to leave

reflexive-verbs.why: Accidents use se, so the thing happens to you.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Accidents: the thing happens to you

reflexive-verbs.why: Negative commands put the pronoun before the verb.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Attached to an affirmative command

reflexive-verbs.why: Parecerse a means to look like.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Parecer to seem, parecerse a to look like

reflexive-verbs.why: Impersonal se means people in general.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Impersonal: people in general, or no specific person

reflexive-verbs.en: We hugged each other at the airport.
reflexive-verbs.why: Plural reflexives can mean each other.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Each other, with plural subjects

reflexive-verbs.en: I fell asleep at the movies.
reflexive-verbs.why: Dormirse means to fall asleep.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Dormir to sleep, dormirse to fall asleep

reflexive-verbs.why: Casarse is reflexive, and ella takes se.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Becoming or changing state

reflexive-verbs.why: Tú takes te.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Me, te, se, nos, and se for ellos and ustedes

reflexive-verbs.q: Mis hijos _____ levantan a las seis.
reflexive-verbs.en: My kids get up at six.
reflexive-verbs.why: Ellos takes se.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Me, te, se, nos, and se for ellos and ustedes

reflexive-verbs.en: What time do you all go to bed?
reflexive-verbs.why: Ustedes takes se, like ellos.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Me, te, se, nos, and se for ellos and ustedes

reflexive-verbs.why: In perfect tenses, the pronoun goes before the whole verb.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Before the whole verb in perfect tenses

reflexive-verbs.why: The pronoun can attach to the gerund, which then takes a written accent.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Attached to an infinitive or gerund, or before the verb in front of it

reflexive-verbs.en: I'm going to go to bed early.
reflexive-verbs.why: Me is already before voy, so the infinitive stays bare.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Attached to an infinitive or gerund, or before the verb in front of it

reflexive-verbs.why: An affirmative command takes the pronoun on the end.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Attached to an affirmative command

reflexive-verbs.q: Todos los días me baño y me _____. (vestir)
reflexive-verbs.en: Every day I bathe and get dressed.
reflexive-verbs.why: Vestirse is part of the daily routine, and vestir changes e to i: me visto.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Daily routine

reflexive-verbs.q: Mi novio y yo _____ escribimos todos los días.
reflexive-verbs.en: My boyfriend and I write to each other every day.
reflexive-verbs.why: With a plural subject, nos can mean each other.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Each other, with plural subjects

reflexive-verbs.en: They looked at each other and smiled.
reflexive-verbs.why: With ellos, se can mean each other.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Each other, with plural subjects

reflexive-verbs.why: Enojarse is to get angry, a change of state.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Becoming or changing state

reflexive-verbs.why: Clothing takes the, not your: ponerse already says whose.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Body parts and clothing take the, not my

reflexive-verbs.why: Llamarse is to be named, and te goes with tú.

possessives.en: His, her, their or your house is very pretty.
choices: any of his, her, their or your
possessives.answer: any of his, her, their or your
possessives.why: Su covers every third person and usted, so context decides.
possessives.rule: Su and suyo can mean his, her, its, their or your

possessives.q: La casa _____ ella es muy bonita.
possessives.why: De ella after the noun makes it clear whose.
possessives.rule: Say de él, de ella or de usted when it isn't clear

possessives.q: ¿Este libro es de él o de _____?
possessives.en: Is this book his or hers?
possessives.why: De ella means hers when suyo would be unclear.
possessives.rule: Say de él, de ella or de usted when it isn't clear

possessives.en: Guys, do you have your tickets yet?
possessives.why: Ustedes takes su. Vuestro is for vosotros, used in Spain.
possessives.rule: Ustedes uses su and suyo too

possessives.why: Ustedes takes suyo, and maletas is feminine plural.
possessives.rule: Ustedes uses su and suyo too

possessives.q: El chico _____ madre es doctora es mi vecino.
possessives.en: The boy whose mother is a doctor is my neighbor.
possessives.why: Cuyo agrees with madre, not with chico.
possessives.rule: Cuyo means whose and agrees with what's owned

possessives.q: La señora _____ hijos viven en Miami es muy amable.
possessives.en: The lady whose children live in Miami is very kind.
possessives.why: It agrees with hijos, masculine plural.
possessives.rule: Cuyo means whose and agrees with what's owned

possessives.why: Questions use de quién. Cuyo only joins sentences.
possessives.rule: In questions, use de quién, not cuyo
